primary.thesis: No formal Israel-Syria security agreement is announced by March 31, and most likely not by June 30 either. As of late January 2026, US-mediated talks (Dermer and al-Shaibani, with Barrack and Witkoff involved, in Paris and Baku) had produced only de-escalation and communication mechanisms, such as the joint coordination cell discussed in early January. Informal steps like that are excluded by the rules. The core gaps are still open: Israel wants a demilitarized south of Syria and to keep its positions in the post-December-2024 buffer zone and on Mount Hermon, and it claims a protector role for the Druze in Sweida. Damascus wants a return to the 1974 disengagement lines and an Israeli withdrawal before signing. Al-Sharaa's government is still consolidating (the SDF integration fight in the northeast, and Alawite and Druze unrest), so it cannot sell a deal at home that looks like giving up territory. Netanyahu, heading into a 2026 election year, has no incentive to withdraw. C1 has only four days left with no signing ceremony signalled, so it is almost certainly NO. For C2 and C3, the bar is a formal, publicly announced, mutually agreed framework, and a process moving this slowly usually misses that bar within five months.

basket.reason: Four days remain, and there is no announced signing, text or summit. The rules also exclude coordination-cell or de-escalation announcements.
The withdrawal and demilitarization gaps and the Druze question are structural. Two months is too short to turn working-level mechanisms into a formal security framework both governments announce.
Israeli election-year politics and Syria's domestic consolidation make a formal deal by mid-2026 less likely than continued incremental arrangements that don't qualify.

failure_narrative: The Trump administration forces a deal as a showcase. Washington offers al-Sharaa sanctions relief, reconstruction money and security guarantees, and gives Netanyahu a diplomatic win before the election, perhaps packaged with Abraham Accords momentum. The two sides then sign a limited 'de-escalation and security arrangement' in the spring. It would restate 1974-style disengagement with phased Israeli pullbacks from new positions and a demilitarized zone south of Damascus, and it would be announced at the White House or in Paris. Because it formally addresses border security, it qualifies. That would lose C3 and possibly C2. A looser risk: one side's official announcement of a 'security understanding', backed by broad credible reporting, is judged to meet the resolution threshold.
hedge_thesis: The worlds where an Israel-Syria deal is signed are worlds where the Trump administration's personal-envoy diplomacy (Witkoff, Kushner, Barrack) is producing signed deals and has the leverage and bandwidth to force hard compromises. That same machinery and style of leverage (sanctions relief traded for territorial or security concessions, deadlines set from the White House) is being applied to Russia-Ukraine. So a Russia-Ukraine ceasefire or framework agreement in the first half of 2026 tends to happen in the same worlds. The two outcomes share a driver: US willingness and ability to push reluctant parties into formal texts. If the deal-making engine is working, both close. If it stalls, both stall. Instruments on a Russia-Ukraine ceasefire, sanctions relief on Russia, or Ukraine reconstruction would pay in the same worlds where my NO basket loses.
